opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it depends a lot on what you want the AI for. There's no law that says intelligent systems have to be like us. Airplanes don't flap their wings, and calculators do arithmetic in a very non-human way, and that's fine. For many narrow applications, replicating human cognition would be beside the point.

But when people talk about "general" intelligence, or systems that we'll interact with, trust, and hand real decisions to, then I think human-like qualities start to matter a lot more. Not because human intelligence is the only possible kind, but because we need these systems to understand the world in ways that are compatible with how we understand it. If a system classifies an image correctly for reasons that have nothing to do with the objects in it, maybe some texture or background cue, it can look intelligent on a benchmark and then fail in bizarre ways when the situation shifts slightly. That brittleness comes partly from the system lacking the kind of conceptual understanding humans have: abstraction, analogy, causal models of the world, common sense about objects and other minds.

So my view is that we don't need to copy the brain or replicate human psychology wholesale. But if we want robust, trustworthy systems that generalize the way we'd expect, we probably need to capture some core aspects of how humans form concepts and make analogies. And honestly, we don't fully understand those things in ourselves yet. That's part of why I find the cognitive science side of this so important. Building AI is in some sense a way of testing our theories of what intelligence even is.

The other thing I'd add is that we should be careful about the reverse problem, which is attributing human-like intelligence to systems that produce human-like outputs. Fluency in language isn't the same as understanding, and we as humans are very prone to anthropomorphizing. So part of thinking clearly about this question is being rigorous about how we evaluate these systems, rather than just being impressed by how human they sound.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm not sure we know what "human-like intelligence" actually is, so the question of whether to replicate it is a bit premature. We have intuitions about it, we have decades of psychology and cognitive science, but we don't have a theory. So when people say they want to build AI that's human-like, they usually mean something narrower than they realize. They mean it should pass certain tests, or produce fluent language, or solve problems the way we'd recognize.

My own view is that there's a lot to be gained from understanding how human intelligence works, and that AI research has historically been a kind of mirror for that. Every time we build a system that does something we thought required intelligence, and it turns out the system is doing it in a shallow way, we learn something about what we were actually assuming. That's been true since the early days of chess programs, and I think it's true now with large language models.

But I'd separate two things. One is replicating human intelligence as a scientific goal, which I find fascinating. The other is replicating it as an engineering goal, and there I'm more skeptical that it's the right target. Humans are good at certain things because of our bodies, our development, our social lives, our evolutionary history. A lot of that may not transfer to a machine, and a lot of it may not even be desirable to transfer. We're biased, we're forgetful, we're bad at probability.

What I do think matters, whether or not the goal is human-like, is the kind of flexible, generalizable understanding that humans have. The ability to take a concept you learned in one setting and apply it in a very different one, to understand what a situation means rather than just matching its surface features. That's what I've spent a lot of my career thinking about, with analogy-making and conceptual abstraction. And I don't think we've cracked that yet, despite how impressive current systems look. So I'd say: don't aim at copying humans, but do pay attention to what humans can do that machines still can't, because that tells you where the real gaps in our understanding are.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we want the AI to do. If we want a system to solve a very specific problem, there’s no reason it has to solve it the way a human would. But if we want systems that can operate flexibly in our world, understand what we mean, and deal with situations they weren’t explicitly trained for, then human intelligence is a very important source of ideas.

That doesn’t mean reproducing every aspect of being human. It means asking which aspects of our intelligence make that flexibility possible. How do we draw on prior experience? How do we recognize that a new situation is similar to something we’ve seen before, but also different in a way that matters?

So I wouldn’t frame it as a choice between copying humans and ignoring humans. We can learn from human intelligence without assuming that it’s the only possible form of intelligence—or that we already understand how it works.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we want the AI to do. If we want a system that can calculate faster than we can, there’s no particular reason it should do that the way humans do. But if we want systems that can operate in our world, interact with us, and understand what we mean, then understanding human intelligence becomes very relevant.

People sometimes point to airplanes and say, well, airplanes don’t flap their wings, so why should AI work like a brain? And that’s fair. We don’t necessarily need to reproduce the mechanisms of human intelligence. But we do need to understand which principles matter. What allows us to take something we’ve learned in one situation and apply it appropriately in a very different situation? How do we know when an analogy is useful and when it breaks down?

So I don’t think human intelligence has to be the endpoint of AI. But it’s the best example we have of the kind of flexible, general intelligence we’re trying to understand. I think dismissing it as irrelevant would be a mistake.
